questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of OSHA’s Hazard Communication Standard?

options.text: To eliminate all chemicals from the workplace
To make sure employees receive information about hazardous chemicals
To require employees to memorize every chemical formula
To replace PPE requirements

questions.questionText: Which three sources communicate chemical hazard information in the workplace?

options.text: Timecards, work orders, and purchase receipts
SDSs, container labels, and the written Hazard Communication Program
Payroll records, inspection tags, and warning lights
Production schedules, maintenance logs, and job descriptions

questions.questionText: True or False: A Safety Data Sheet provides detailed information about a chemical’s hazards, PPE, storage, first aid, and spill response.

options.text: True
False

options.text: Smell it to identify it
Use it only if it looks familiar
Do not use it and report it
Pour it into a drain

options.text: Inhalation
Skin contact
Ingestion
All of the above

The amount of chemical a person is exposed to
The number of containers in storage
The age of the chemical

options.text: True
False

options.text: They may release vapors that can ignite
They are always harmless unless swallowed
They do not require labels
They cannot be stored in cabinets

options.text: The SDS and container label
The color of the container

Flush the eyes immediately at an eyewash station
Finish the task first
Wipe the eyes with a dry cloth

questions.questionText: Who should clean up a hazardous chemical spill?

options.text: Any nearby employee
Only employees who are trained, authorized, and properly protected
The newest employee
Anyone wearing safety glasses

Clean water
Plain cardboard
Compressed air only

options.text: Saving production time
Protecting people’s health and safety
Finding someone to blame
Cleaning the spill as fast as possible without PPE

lessons.hazcom-overview: OSHA’s Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200) is built on the right to know: workers cannot protect themselves from chemical hazards they are not aware of. The standard requires employers to maintain a written Hazard Communication Program, ensure containers are labeled, make Safety Data Sheets accessible, and train all employees who may be exposed to hazardous chemicals. Three core elements deliver chemical hazard information: SDSs, container labels, and the written program. Training must cover where to find this information, how to use it, and what to do if an exposure or spill occurs.
lessons.safety-data-sheets: A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is the primary technical reference for a hazardous chemical. Organized into 16 standardized sections under the Globally Harmonized System (GHS), an SDS covers physical and chemical properties, health and physical hazards, first aid measures, firefighting procedures, spill and leak response, handling and storage requirements, PPE and exposure controls, and emergency contacts. Section 8 identifies required PPE; Section 7 covers safe handling and storage; Section 4 describes first aid steps. SDSs must be accessible to every employee during every work shift in a language they can understand. Consult the SDS before using any unfamiliar chemical.
lessons.container-labels: Every container of hazardous chemicals must display a label identifying the chemical, its hazards, and the manufacturer. GHS-compliant labels include pictograms that communicate hazard categories visually, a signal word (Danger or Warning), hazard statements, and precautionary statements. When a chemical is transferred into a secondary container — such as a spray bottle, squeeze bottle, or bucket — that container must also be labeled unless the employee who transferred it will use all contents immediately during that shift. Unlabeled containers must not be used. Report missing or damaged labels to a supervisor immediately.
lessons.written-program: The written Hazard Communication Program documents how the employer implements the HazCom standard at the facility. It must identify who is responsible for maintaining SDSs and container labels, describe how employees are trained, explain how chemical inventory is tracked, and address how contractors are informed about chemical hazards on site. Employees have the right to access and review the written program at any time. A complete and current written program demonstrates that chemical safety is actively managed — not just assumed — and provides a framework for consistent compliance across the facility.
lessons.chemical-hazards: Hazardous chemicals present physical hazards (flammability, reactivity, explosivity, compressed gas) or health hazards (toxicity, corrosivity, carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity). Flammable liquids release vapors at or near room temperature that can travel to an ignition source and flash back, causing fire or explosion. Carcinogens may not cause symptoms for years or decades after exposure, making early recognition and reporting critical. Corrosives destroy tissue on contact. The SDS Section 2 identifies hazard classifications for a specific chemical and summarizes the types of harm exposure may cause. Understanding hazard classes helps workers recognize when extra precautions are needed.
lessons.exposure-routes: Chemicals enter the body through four routes: inhalation (breathing vapors, dust, fumes, or mist), skin and eye contact (absorption through skin or splashing into eyes), ingestion (swallowing — typically from contaminated hands near the mouth), and injection (rare, from a puncture with a contaminated sharp). Risk depends on the dose (how much), duration (how long), frequency of exposure, route of entry, and the chemical’s toxicity. Even small repeated exposures can accumulate over time. Wearing the correct PPE, using ventilation controls, and following safe handling procedures reduces all four exposure pathways.
lessons.ppe-controls: Engineering controls — ventilation, enclosed processes, substitution — are the first line of defense against chemical exposure. When engineering controls are insufficient, PPE is required. The SDS Section 8 specifies the type of gloves, eye protection, respiratory protection, and protective clothing needed for a given chemical. Glove material matters: some chemicals permeate certain glove types rapidly, providing no real protection. Always check the SDS and container label before selecting PPE for any chemical task. Never rely on a coworker’s judgment or past practice alone — chemical compatibility must be verified against the specific substance being handled.
lessons.storage-handling: Chemicals must be stored to minimize hazards: flammables in approved flammable storage cabinets away from ignition sources, incompatibles segregated (acids from bases, oxidizers from flammables), and quantities limited to what is needed. Containers must remain tightly closed when not in use. Secondary containers must be labeled. Chemicals must never be stored near food, beverages, or medications. The SDS Section 7 provides specific storage and handling requirements for each chemical. Proper storage prevents accidental reactions, reduces fire and explosion risk, and ensures that containers remain in good condition with labels intact.
lessons.exposure-response: When a chemical spill occurs, the first priority is protecting people — not cleaning the spill. Employees who are not trained and equipped for spill response should evacuate the area, alert others, and call for trained responders. Only trained employees with appropriate PPE should handle cleanup. If a chemical contacts skin or eyes, flush immediately with water for at least 15 minutes at an eyewash or emergency shower. All exposures — even ones that seem minor — must be reported immediately so medical evaluation can be obtained and an investigation can identify the source. Delayed reporting can complicate treatment and prevent hazard correction.

1.questionText: Under OSHA’s Hazard Communication Standard, what is the employer required to ensure?

options.text: Chemicals are eliminated from all production processes
Employees receive information and training about hazardous chemicals they may be exposed to
All chemical containers are color-coded for quick identification
Employees memorize the chemical formula of every substance used on site

2.questionText: Which combination of resources forms the core of OSHA’s Hazard Communication system?

options.text: Purchase orders, shipping manifests, and work orders
Safety Data Sheets, container labels, and the written Hazard Communication Program
Verbal shift briefings, inspection reports, and MSDS cards
Safety incentive boards, PPE closets, and chemical color codes

3.questionText: True or False: Safety Data Sheets are organized into 16 standardized GHS sections and must be accessible to employees during all work shifts.

options.text: True
False

4.questionText: A container in the work area has no label and the contents are unknown. What is the safest immediate action?

options.text: Open it carefully and smell the contents to identify the substance
Set it aside and assume it will be relabeled later
Test a small amount on a work surface before using
Do not use it, keep it closed, and report it to a supervisor

5.questionText: A worker absorbs a harmful solvent through the skin while wiping down a surface without gloves. Which route of entry applies?

options.text: Inhalation
Skin absorption
Ingestion
Injection

6.questionText: Two workers are exposed to the same chemical. Worker A is exposed for 30 minutes; Worker B for 4 hours. Which factor most increases Worker B’s risk?

options.text: The odor strength of the chemical
The container color
The duration of exposure
The number of containers in the storage area

7.questionText: True or False: If a worker notices redness after brief chemical contact but feels no pain, no report is needed.

options.text: True
False

8.questionText: A drum of flammable liquid is stored near an electrical panel. Why is this a serious hazard?

options.text: Flammable liquids are always corrosive and will damage the panel
Flammable liquids release vapors that can be ignited by electrical sparks
Flammable liquids cannot be stored in metal drums
The panel will contaminate the liquid and make it more toxic

9.questionText: Before performing a chemical handling task, which reference should an employee consult to determine the correct PPE?

options.text: The production supervisor’s verbal preference
The last inspection checklist
The SDS and container label for the specific chemical
A general PPE guide from a previous task

10.questionText: An employee pours acetone from a large drum into an unlabeled quart jar for use at a workstation. What is required before the jar can be used?

options.text: Nothing — only the original drum needs a label
The jar must be labeled with the chemical identity and hazard warnings
The jar must be left open so the contents can be identified by smell
The jar must be stored under a supervisor’s desk until needed

11.questionText: Chemical vapor gets into a worker’s eyes during a spray application. What should the worker do immediately?

options.text: Rinse the eyes briefly with drinking water and continue working
Go to a break room and wait for symptoms to subside
Flush both eyes continuously at an eyewash station and seek medical attention
Apply eye drops from the first aid kit and return to work

12.questionText: A drum of corrosive cleaner cracks and leaks across the floor. Which employees should respond to the spill?

options.text: The first employee to notice it, regardless of training
The shift supervisor only, directing cleanup from a distance
The nearest available employees, since speed is most important
Only those trained, authorized, and equipped with proper PPE for that chemical

13.questionText: True or False: Employees are entitled to access the facility’s written Hazard Communication Program to understand how chemical safety is managed.

options.text: True
False

14.questionText: A worker has used a chemical for two years with no obvious symptoms. The SDS lists it as a suspected carcinogen. What should the worker understand?

options.text: Carcinogens always cause immediate reactions, so no past symptoms means no risk
Carcinogen exposure carries long-term health risks even without current symptoms and should be reported
Carcinogen warnings on SDSs are required by law but rarely apply at real exposure levels
No symptoms over two years confirms the worker is not at risk

15.questionText: A chemical container is knocked over and begins leaking. What should happen first?

options.text: Contain the spill using the nearest available absorbent material
Protect people’s health and safety — alert others and evacuate if not trained for spill response
Identify the responsible party so a corrective action report can be filed
Clean the spill as quickly as possible to prevent production delays
